title: Private networking workshop — quick playbook and POC notes
content:
Purpose / audience:
This is a compact workshop playbook and live-notes doc for SE-run customer POCs that involve exposing Redwood Private endpoints into a customer VPC or integrating a customer VPC with Redwood’s private control plane. Audience: SEs, customer infra architects, platform engineers.

Context & prerequisites observed during recent runs:
- Most customers are multi-account AWS (prod/staging/shared-services) behind an org-level Transit Gateway or use isolated peering per account.
- Common constraints: no public ingress allowed, strict CIDR non-overlap requirements, mandatory egress inspection (proxy/firewall), and DNS split-horizon must resolve Redwood service names internally.
- Typical requirement: reach Redwood Private control plane over private networking (no public IPs), TLS required, optional mTLS for control plane, and limited IP allowlist.

Design goals for the POC:
- Minimum blast radius: avoid changing prod route tables; use a sandbox/shared-services VPC if possible.
- Simple to demo quickly (30–90 min): prioritize solutions that require minimal infra changes but show full end-to-end (network, DNS, auth).
- Reproducible for customers to harden after POC (clear handoff guidance).

Common architecture options (short comparison):
1) VPC Peering + Interface Endpoints
   - What: Peer customer VPC(s) to a Redwood-managed VPC and use interface ENIs/NLBs for service exposure.
   - Pros: Simple, low-latency, easy to reason about. Works in same region only.
   - Cons: Scales poorly across many accounts/regions, requires distinct route table entries per peering, CIDR must not overlap.
   - When to use: small POCs, single-account demos, customers with no TGW.

2) Transit Gateway (TGW) + Shared Services VPC
   - What: Attach customer account(s) to a TGW and create a shared-services VPC where Redwood endpoints (internal NLB/ENIs) live.
   - Pros: Scales across many accounts/regions (if Transit Gateway peering used), centralized routing and inspection, easier hub-and-spoke.
   - Cons: More setup (TGW attachments, route propagation), possible cost/approval friction for customers.
   - When to use: enterprise customers with TGW already in place or multiple accounts to connect.

3) AWS PrivateLink / EndpointService (recommended for hardened private exposure)
   - What: Redwood exposes an EndpointService (NLB fronted) and customer creates an Interface VPC Endpoint (com.amazonaws.vpce).
   - Pros: No route table changes, works cross-account, preserves isolation, built-in AWS private connectivity semantics, easier security review for some customers.
   - Cons: ENI provisioning in customer subnets (IP consumption), costs for endpoints, additional DNS glue may be required.
   - When to use: customers that cannot accept peering or TGW changes, or need cross-account private connectivity pattern.

DNS patterns and recommendations:
- Requirement: internal resolution must map redwood-controlled hostnames to private IPs (interface endpoints / internal NLBs).
- Options:
  1) Conditional forwarder / Route53 Resolver inbound endpoints: customer forwards queries for redwood.internal (or customer-specific zone) to Redwood’s resolver. Use inbound endpoints in the customer VPC so Redwood can resolve customer private hostnames if needed.
  2) Private hosted zone delegation: Redwood provides a private hosted zone owned by customer (delegated) so names resolve in customer VPCs.
  3) Modify /etc/hosts or local DNS entries (fast hack for POC only).
- Recommendation for POC: use Route53 Resolver rules + inbound endpoint for two-way resolution only if customer infra permits. For the quickest path, provide the IPs of the interface endpoints and ask customer to add A records in their private zone.

Ingress / endpoints specifics:
- Use an internal NLB in the Redwood side if we need stable IPs; present the NLB as an EndpointService for PrivateLink. NLB preserves TCP passthrough (recommended to keep TLS end-to-end).
- For control-plane APIs: TCP 443 (HTTPS). For internal debug channels (if any), document additional ports.
- Provide a minimal /28 per interface endpoint to avoid IP exhaustion during the demo (we typically reserve 4–16 IPs depending on AZs).

Egress & internet-bound traffic:
- Customers often require egress inspection. Options: NAT Gateway per AZ, centralized egress through a firewall/proxy (Zscaler, Palo Alto), or an egress VPC with inspection appliances behind TGW.
- For POC, two pragmatic approaches:
  1) Use NAT GW in demo VPCs (fast, default).
  2) If customer mandates inspection, route egress via their proxy and provide a small allowlist for Redwood control-plane hostnames/ips.
- Recommend adding S3/ECR Gateway endpoints (s3/vpc endpoint) to avoid routing large pulls through NAT/proxy.

Security groups / ACLs / minimal firewall rules:
- Security group on Redwood endpoint: allow inbound 443 from customer VPC CIDRs / interface endpoint SG. Lock to specific account CIDRs when possible.
- Customer SG: allow outbound 443 to Redwood endpoint SG.
- NACLs: generally keep permissive for the demo (stateful SGs suffice), but call out NACL hardening in handoff doc.

CIDR and IP planning notes (examples for POC):
- Suggested sandbox plan (non-overlapping):
  - shared-services VPC (Redwood-facing) 10.64.0.0/20
  - customer-demo VPC (app) 10.32.0.0/20
  - ingress endpoint subnets (per AZ) /28 each for interface endpoints
- Call out overlapping networks early in workshop checklist — stop the run if overlapping is discovered until resolved.

Operational concerns & metrics to validate in POC:
- Latency: measure p95/P99 for token call roundtrip (control-plane handshake and model start). Capture baseline with public vs private path.
- Failover: simulate NLB/endpoint AZ failure and verify automatic failover.
- Throughput: test small burst of concurrent connections to validate SG, ENI, and NLB limits.
- DNS: show that resolution is stable and TTLs behave as expected when we flip IPs.

Quick workshop runbook (30–90m):
1) Pre-meeting: collect CIDR ranges, account IDs, contact for infra approvals, whether TGW/PrivateLink allowed, DNS owner.
2) 0–15m: Align on chosen architecture (PrivateLink vs TGW vs Peering). Confirm SG/IPs.
3) 15–45m: Provision endpoints (Redwood creates EndpointService or NLB, customer creates Interface Endpoint) OR attach TGW and add route entries.
4) 45–60m: DNS mapping (customer creates A records for provided ENI IPs OR configure resolver rules).
5) 60–80m: Smoke tests: curl/openssl s_client to 443, run a short inference request, validate logs and tracing.
6) 80–90m: Capture output (latency numbers, errors), capture screenshots, agree next steps.

Open questions for customer (short checklist to capture during kickoff):
- Do you allow cross-account PrivateLink? (yes/no)
- Are CIDR ranges available that do not overlap with Redwood default ranges? Provide list.
- Is there a corporate egress proxy/firewall that will block outbound to AWS PrivateLink endpoints?
- Is DNS admin willing to create private records or Route53 Resolver rules for the POC?
- Do you require mutual TLS or client certs for control-plane APIs?

Action items (owners & targets):
- Aditi: prepare NLB + EndpointService template and example CloudFormation snippet (due: 2026-02-20).
- Matt: sample Route53 Resolver rule + inbound endpoint runbook and minimal IAM perms (due: 2026-02-22).
- Evelyn: test script for smoke tests (curl + small client inference, automated), include capture of p50/p95/p99 (due: 2026-02-25).
- Diego: collect customer CIDR list and validate for overlap prior to the workshop (ASAP).

Notes / fringe cases seen in prior customers:
- Some corporate firewalls block AWS-managed ENI traffic based on deep packet or DNS heuristics; have a fallback plan to run a short demo with tunnelled SSH port-forward (last resort).
- GCP customers prefer Private Service Connect over peering; similar pattern, but DNS/ACL details differ — note vendor-specific quirks during handoffs.
- If the customer refuses ENIs in app subnets (IP consumption concern), propose a small dedicated subnet just for interface endpoints (/28).

References & templates to attach to customer handoff:
- CloudFormation snippet for EndpointService + NLB (attach link)
- Customer-side Interface Endpoint creation template (CloudFormation + CLI)
- Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound sample commands and minimal IAM policy statements

Last thoughts (keep in mind during demos):
- Start with the minimal path that satisfies customer security constraints — don’t overcomplicate the first demo.
- Capture the exact infra changes in the run (screenshots of console, config snippets) — customers want a repeatable playbook.
- If the customer will move to production, recommend a formal security review and prefer PrivateLink or TGW depending on scale and governance.

End of doc — iterate after next POC.
